Why don't the men propose, mamma ? Why don't the men propose? Each seems coming to the point, And then away lie goes ! It is no fault of your's, mamma, That every body knows ; Y ou fete the finest men in town, Yet, oh ! they won't propose ?

I'm sure I've done my best, mamma, To make a proper match ; For coronets and eldest sons I'm ever on the watch ; I've hopes when some distingue beau A glance upon me throws ; But though he'll dance, and smile, and flirt, Alas ! he won't propose !

I've tried to win by languishing And dressing like a blue ; I've bought big books, and talk'd of them As if I'd read them through ! With hair cropp'd like a man I've felt The heads of all the beaux ; But Spurzheim could not touch their hearts, And oh ! they won't propose !

I threw aside the books and thought That ignorance was bliss ; I felt convinced that men preferred A simple sort of Miss ; And so 1 lisp'd< out naught beyond Plain "yeses" or plain "noes," And wore a sweet unmeaning smile ; Yet, oh, they won't propose !

Last night, at Lady Ramble's rout, Exclaim, " Now I propose again I heard Sir Harry Gale 1 started, turning pale ; I really thought my time was come, 1 blush'd like like any rose; But oh ! I found 'twas only at Eearte he'd propose !

And what is to be done, mamma ? Oh, what is to be done ? I really have no time to lose, For 1 am thirty-one ; At balls I am too often left Where spinsters sit in rows ; Why won't the men propose, mamma ? Why won't the men propose?

An extraordinary birth occurred in this town yesterday. A young negro woman, in the service of a Miss Frances Phillippart, residing in (Jhariestown district, was delivered of a still-born child with two heads and four arms. The bodies are separate to the chest, where they unite in one trunk, which, together with the lower extremities, presents no deviation from the usual course of nature. The two outer arms are perfect, but the two between the heads are inclined backwards. The child is of a remarkably large size, and caused so painful a labour that the mother is not expected to survive. We have not heard whether the body is to be dissected, but imagine that the opportunity of becoming acquainted with the details of so remarkable a conformation will not be suflered to pass unnoticed. þÿ Demerara Royal Gazette, October 30.

Uncertainty of Life. When the news of the demise of his late Majesty George IV. reached Marlow, an elderly lady hustled oil' to all the shops in the town, to look for mourning ; this occupied some time, and she requested the principal linen-draper of the place, it then being her dinner hour, to allow the black goods she had been inspecting to remain on his counter for an hour, when she promised to return and make her final arrangements about them. In the evening, singular to relate, these same goods were all sent to the house of this lady, that her relations might purchase their mourning for her, she having suddenly expired when at dinner !

Dumerg, the celebrated dentist, having the children of a late naval officer under his care for their teeth, which required expensive operations, upon learning that their widowed mother was left in a very destitute condition, steadily refused payment the young people. " God forbid," said this for his services to humane surgeon, ' that I should take a sous from the scanty pittance of the widows and orphans of those brave men whose toils, struggles, and very lives, have merely sufficed to gain it. No ! young people bereaved like these are the children of their country, and as such fully entitled, I consider, to my services, at least, without cost."
comet. The 1 1 alley Gomel is now visible in the l East, near the constellation Taurus. At this

time its distance from the earth is forty millions of miles. On the 13th of September . will be only twenty-two millions of miles distant, and from this will become brilliant. In, the latter part of September it will enter the Twins, and on the 1st of October will reach within six millions of miles of us, the four feet of the Great Bear, where it no more sets. At this its brilliance and apparent magnitude will have arrived at the highest degree. On the Oth October it will stand nearest the earth, only three and a half millions of miles distant. In the beginning of the year 1836, it will emerge from the sun beams, and again become visible at the distance of forty millions of miles from us. It will for second time approach the earth, and on the 1st of March, 1836, will stand twenty-five millions of miles distant. Thence it will recede from the earth, and seem to wander 76 years; and in the year 1912, will again visit our regions. þÿ New lark Commercial Advertiser.

Presence of Mind. þÿ There was a party of gentlemen and ladies who went to visit Redlam, and, as they were going through the wards, one of the gentlemen was accosted by a person whom he supposed to be one ot the keepers, and who said to him in a whisper, þÿ Your friends are only going through the common parts of the establishment, but i. ou 1 will come with me, 1 will show you the apartments which are not generally opened to þÿstrangers. The man went off and beckoned to the gentleman, yvho stepped away from bis companions, tofolloyv bis new guide, who led him through sundry passages to the top of the building, and then out upon the leads. No sooner were they there than the man said to the gentleman, þÿ Now, sir, jump into the street þÿ! You may suppose what were his feelings when he found himself in the presence of a madman, and kneyv that the þÿmadman s next step would probably be to throw him off the building. But his piesenee of mind suggested a means ot escape, and he said to the madman, þÿ Jump down! Anybody can jump down; but it you 11 let me, þÿI go ll down & jump up, which will be much more ofa feat." The madman Durst into a laugh, þÿ Ha ! ha! indeed it will; march doyvn and þÿtry. So the gentleman was allowed to go; and naturally the first thing he did was to inlbrm the keepers of the narrow escape he had had, and to urge them to be a little more careful in future that such a dangerous lunatic should not be allowed to put þÿpeople l s ives in jeopardy. þÿ Dr. Bowring's Minor Murals.

THE LATE DUKE OF GLOUCESTER. The Governors of the London Hospital, to manifest their respect for the memory, and their regret at the loss which the charity has sustained by the death of their late illustrious President, who had filled that office for nearly 30 years, attended Divine Service, in the Chapel of the Institution, on Sunday, the 14th inst., when an appropriate and impressive sermon was preached by the Chaplain, the Reverend Mr. Valentine, who took his text on the occasion from Job xxix., verse 11, 10, arid first clause of verse 13. The Reverend þÿGentleman allusion s to the interesting spectacle of an audience such as the one he was addressing, composed of the supporters and the objects of Christian benevolence þÿ assembled too for the purpose of paying a tribute of respect to the memory of a most distinguished benefactor þÿ was received in a manner at once in the highest degree gratifying and affecting. Among those present were observed the Treasurer, the Chairman of the House Committee and other distinguished Governors and friends,

The Chapel was deeply hung with black, and Other emblems of departed rank. Many anecdotes are told of the good feel, ing repeatedly exemplified by the late Duke of Gloucester, particularly towards the poor in his own immediate neighbourhood Among j others the following may he relied on as one highly redounding to his Royal Highness's I kind-heartedness: þÿ A few years since an industrious broom dasher had erected a hut on a piece of waste ground in the vicinity of Bagshot, which he held on sufferance for a considerable period; in fact no notice was taken of his domicile until an application was made to Parliament for an Inclosure Bill, which would embrace the ground occupied hv the poor fellow, when he was told he must decamp. Oppressed with disappointment, he made his case known to the Duke, who. feeling for his distressed situation, said he would see what couid be done for him. His Royal Highness accordingly attended the Commissioners previously to making the award, and not only advocated his right not to be disturbed in his possession but maintained that he was entitled to a proportionate allotment of land in right of his occupation, and this was actually granted. þÿ Windsor Express.

þÿLONGEVITY. OLD PARR. By a wise provision of the great Author of our being, we are fond of life, and desirous as tar as we can, of extending the short span allotted to us on earth. For this purpose, health, which forms a large ingredient in human happiness, must bo promoted ; and whatever tends to health, tends also to old age. þÿ When, therefore, we m >et with persons who have reached their eightieth or ninetieth vear, or read of those whose age has amounted to a hundred and upwards, it is no less instructive than interesting to observe the means, which under Providence, have led to their arriving at such an advanced period of life. It will generally be found, on inquiry into such cases, that certain modes of living have been adopted, which nay be called some of the conditions of longevity; and the tallies which have been given of the respective ages and residences of certain very aged persons, with some sketch of their history, establish this fact, with few exceptions. They have, almost all, been born of healthy parents, and

&A.U3X T33in3TI»33X 3i3&XJmxrt>3 AT33. have been early accustomed to exercise, tem- I I perance and simplicity of food. To these may be added, in the greater number of instances, early rising, and a due regulation of those passions which are bestowed on man for good and wise ends ; hut which, when abused, invariably hasten on his decay. With these remarks, which we trust may prove acceptable to some of our readers, we have prefaced a short account of the celebrated Thomas Parr, or, as he is called, in a portrait of his own time. þÿ The old, old, very old man, of Wilmington, in the parish of Alderbury, in Shropshire ; who was horn in the reign of King Edward the Fourth, in the year 14N3. He lived 152 years, 9 months, and odd days, and departed this life at Westminster, Nov. 15, þÿ1(535. There is hut little mentioned of his life ; hut perhaps, the most remarkable incident in it was tlie occasion of his being brought from his native village to London. Thomas carl of Arundell and Surrey, earl marshal of England, was visiting some manors which he held together with the officers of the Charity. þÿ in Shropshire; and, hearing of þÿParr g s reat age, he proposed to him a journey to London. The earl accordingly provided a litter and two horses for him ; and, with some difficulty, in consequence of the crowds of people who pressed to see the old man, got him safe to London, where he was well entertained at his þÿlordship cost. s The following amusing anecdote is told of him: þÿ His three leases of 21 years each,

making (53 years, having expired, lie took his last lease of his landlord, Mr. John Porter, for his life, with which lease he lived more than fifty years. But he wished, for his w þÿife s sake, to renew his lease for years, which his landlord would not consent to; upon which Old Parr, who had long been blind, and was sitting in his chair bv the fire, being told by hi- wife that young Mr. Porter, the þÿlandlord s son, was coming towards the house to call: þÿ Is lie þÿso, said Parr, þÿ 1 prithee, wife, lav a pin on the ground near my foot, or at my right þÿtoe, which she did ; and when young Mr. Porter came, the old man said, after the usual salutations. þÿ Wife, is not that a pin that lies at my þÿfoot! þÿ Truly þÿhusband, (quoth she,) þÿ it is a pin, indeed þÿ! so she took it up, and Air. Porter was amazed that the old man had recovered his sight again; but it was quickly found to he þÿ a witty conceit, thereby to have him suppose him to be more lively than lie was, because he hoped to have his lease renewed for his þÿwife þÿsake. s Tlie longevity of Thomas Parr seems to have descended as an heir-loom to his posterity: as his son lived to the age of 113, his grandson to 109, and his great grandson to 121 ! Perhaps the most extraordinary instance on record of liveliness , such as is shown in the anecdote above, at an extreme old age, is that ol tlie Countess of Desmond, who died 140 years old. Her death happened at tlie end of Queen þÿElizabeth reign, s it was said at the time, þÿ by a fever occasioned by a fall from

Ant Plague in Grenada. þÿ 'The numbers were so immense as to cover tlie roads for þÿth( space of several miles ; and so crowded in many places that the prints of the horses feet were distinctly marked amongst them till filled by the surrounding multitude. They made bridges across large and rapid rivers with the dead bodies of their comrades Every kind of cold victuals, ail species of vermin,

particularly rats, and even the sores of the I negroes were exposed to their attacks. A premium of £20,000 from the public Treasury was offered to the discoverer of any effectual method of destroying them, and the principal means employed were poison and fire. By mixing arsenic and corrosive sublimate with animal substances, myriads wore destroyed ; and the slightest tasting of the poison rendered them so outrageous as to devour one another Lines of red hot charcoal were laid in their way, to which they crowded iu such numbers as to extinguish it with their bodies ; and holes full of fire were dug in the cane grounds, which were soon extinguished by heaps of dead. But while the nests remained undisturbed, new progenies appeared as numerous as ever, and the only effectual check which they received was from the destructive hurricane, which by tearing up altogether, or so loosening the roots of the plants where they nestled, so as to admit the rain, almost extirpated the whole race. þÿ history of the British Colonies.

TSIsMTOST® 13IRL JMfcXERlSma &T33 &2L&3 CATS TRIALS OF GUILT IN SUPERSTITIOUS AGES. It is melancholy to reflect on the strange trials to which, in remoter ages, those suspected of guilt were put. The Ordeal con- j sisted of various kinds; walking blindfold amidst red-hot ploughshares, placed at unequal distances; passing through two fires; holding in the hand a red-hot liar; plunging the hand into boiling water ; challenging the accuser to single combat : the swallowing a morsel of consecrated bread ; the sinking or swimming in a river in tire case of witchcraft, and v arious others. þÿ One cannot (says the learned and excellent Bluekstonc,) but be astonished and surprised at the folly and impiety of pronouncing a man guilty unless lie was cleared bv a minicle : and of expecting that all ihe powers of nature should be suspended by an immediate interposition of providence to save the innocent whenever it was presumptuously required. And yet in England, so late as King John's time, we lind grants to the bishops and clergy to use the þÿ trial by iron, fire, and water." But though they used to preside at these trials, which were performed in churches, or in other consecrated ground; yet the Canon Law very early declared against trial by ordeal, as the fabric of Satan : and it was abolished in England by Act oi Parliament or rather by an order of the King in Council, in the reign of Henry the Third. Fire ordeal was performed either by taking up in the hand unhurt, a piece of red-hot iron, of one, two, or three pounds weight:

or else by walking blindiold and barefoot over nine red-hot ploughshares, laid, lengthwise, at unequal distances; audit the party escaped unhurt, he was adjudged innocent; but if it happened otherwise, as without collusion it usually did, he was then condemned guiltv. Q.: u Emma the mother oi Edward the Confessor, when suspected, is mentioned to have cleared her character by this latter meth d. Water ordeal was performed either by plungin;.' the i are arm up to the elbow in boiling water, and escaping unhurt; or by casting the pei si hi suspected into a river or pond; and f he floated : herein, without any action oi swimming, it was deemed an evidence oi his guilt ; but if lie sunk, he was acquitted. It is said that secrets were known in those times, by which these trials might be passed unhurt; particularly' with regard to the ordeal oi boiling water, we are told, they used to rub their arm a long time with the spirit oi vitriol and j alum, together with the juice of an onion. We cannot vouch for the truth of this recipe. The trial of Bread was thus conducted. A piece oi bread or oi cheese, was consecrated (how shockingly degrading was such superstition !) with a prayer, desiring the Almighty that it might cause convulsions and paleness, and lind no passage, if the man was guilty ; | but might turn to health and nourishment it he was innocent. This piec e of bread, called the eorsned, or morsel of cursing, was then given to the suspected person. Our historians assure us, that Godwin, Earl of Kenl, in

the rcigh of Edward the Confessor, adjuring the death of the king's brother, appealed to his eorsned, which stuck in his throat, and killed him. Though this custom has been long abolished, we are too often reminded oi it by the very unwarrantable language of in-

considerate people, in such phrases as May þÿ this morsel be my last þÿ May this piece of bread choke þÿme! The super itious people who practised this mode oi tr nl, were very particular in the making oi this bread and cheese. The bread was to be of unleavened barley; and the cheese made of ewe milk in the month of May; no other oi ihe vvelvemontlis having any power to detect a criminal. Another most extraordinary trial, was that of þÿ the bleeding of a þÿcorpse. If a person w as murdered, it was said, that at the touchy or at the approach of the murderer, the blood would gush out of the body at various parts. This was once allowed in England, and is still looked on, in some uncivilized parts, as a detection of the criminal. V\ e trust such remains of credulity and superstition are rapidþÿly passing away, never to return. These trials of ordeal were mostly oi Faxon origin : the trial by battel, or single combat, was derived from the Normans.

Prejudice, the Spider of the þÿMind. Of Prejudice it has been truly said, that it has the singular ability of accomodating itself to all the possible varieties of human þÿmind. Some passions and vices are but thinly scattered among mankind, and find only here and there a fitness of reception. But prejudice, like the spider, makes every where its home. It has neither taste nor choice of place, and all that it requires is room. There is scarcely a situation, except tire and water, in which a spider will not live. So let the mind be as naked as the walls of an empty and lbrsaken tenement, gloomy as a dungeon, or ornamented with the richest abilities ot thinking: let it be hot, cold, dark, or light, lonely or inhabited, still prejudice, if undisturbed, will fill it with cobwebs and live, like the spider, where there seems nothing to live on. Jf the one prepares

her food by poisoning it to her palate and her use, the other does the same ; and as several of our passions are strongly characterised by the animal world, prejudice may be denominated the Spider ol the Mind. þÿ Retrospective Review.

The civil (Joints in Paris have been lately occupied with rather a curious case of claims from three widows to the pension of one husband, which were made under the following circumstances: þÿ So long ago as the 30th of July, 1.70, a person named Ward, then a merchant, Out afterwards a Colonel upon the Suit! of the French Army, married at Bayonne a certain Miss S. Being of an extravagant turn, he soon squandered his own and his þÿwile s fortune, abandoned her, and went to the colonies. There he again married a Miss Pauline de C., whom, alter living with a few years, he also deserted and returned to France, not to Ins first wife, however, but to wed a third, the Demoiselle Virginie G. In lSjg this Don Juan died, leaving the pension of a General U u :er to be scrambled tor ainongs, his widows. come from his landed property in the Roman estates and in Bavaria is above (518,000 guilders, or 00,0001. It has been erroneously stated in some of the journals, that the Prince has not seen Donna Maria, or his sister, the Duchess of Braganza, since 1829, when he escorted the latter to the Brazils. This is not correct. In 18- >i, when Don Pedro left Paris to undertake the xpeuition to Terceira, the Duke of Leuch- i tenburg was then on a visit to his sister, and it

was during his stay there that Donna Maria formed the strong attachment she has evinced, for him. A man having been long troubled by the repeated intrusions ot the log of a neighbouring storekeeper, at length resolved to rid himself of the nuisance by his own ingenuity, as his remonstrances with the owner were likely to prove unavailing. He accordingly procured a cylinder of tin, half an inch in diameter, and about three in length þÿ this lie nearly filled with powder and placed on the top a small piece of touchwood, enveloped the tube in a piece of fat pork, and threw it into the street. Poor Jowler seized and swallowed the dainty morsel; and thus primed and loaded, returned to his master's store, which was well filled with ladies and gentlemen purchasing goods, where he soon exploded ! þÿ With a tremendous report, which shook the whole building and alarmed all the citizens in the neighbourhood, poor Jowler was blown into ten thousand atoms, which were equally distributed in every part of the

shop I The ladies were covered with the bleeding fragments of the dog, and one of them had her cheek terribly scratched by the claws of one of his hind legs, as it whizzed like a double headed shot past her ear. A portion of the spine struck Mr. Smith, the owner, in the forehead, and laid him sprawling. His clerk rushed to the door, his clothes and features bespattered with blood, and screamed þÿ fire! and þÿ murder! right manfully. The ladies joined in the chorus, the bells wore set a ringing, and the people rapidly assembled and gazed with hoiror and consternation on this unparalleled scene of blood and carnage. þÿ Philadelphia Commercial Herald.

Ezekiel Law , the. Water þÿDrinker. A many provincial and other papers have copied a slight yet erroneous notice, vve have been favoured with the following account from the pen of a person who has for many years past had an opportunity of witnessing the habits and occupation of this singular and remarkable mail. Ezekiel Law died on b i nlay, the 3d of October, 1834, at Fulbourn, aged 44 years. He has had, from the age of five or six years, a propensity or insatiable desire lor drinking cold water, and lias continued drinking the amazing quantity of 14 quaits every 21 hours until a short time before bis death. He generally took about two gallons of cold water to his bedside every night, and has bad the same desire for water in summer and winter ; if without cold water a few hours either night or day, he felt uneasiness in his throat and stomach ; and if without for some time, and he drank beer or any other beverage before he had first drank a portion of cold water, it did not agree upon his stomach. I pon a moderate calculation he has drank the astonishing quantity of 35 barrels, 17 gallons in a year, amounting to 1330$ barrels in 28 years.

UNDER protection of Divine Providence, and in obedience to the command of our most gracious Sovereign, 1 am once more allbrded the pleasure of being placed among you, my fellow subjects, in order to exert myself sincerely, and candidly to preserve peace and tranquility in His þÿMajesty s Colonies, and promote the prosperity thereof. This object l am well aware cannot be obtained, but by your mutual assistance and your conlidence in my measures, and from my experience during the number of years 1 have been intrusted with the administration of this Island, 1 feel conlidcut 1 shall want neither. In regard to owners of slaves and their agents, it is scarcely necessary lor me to recommend a continuance of the humane and prudent conduct towards those under their charge, which of late years, at the same time it conferred honor on the masters, lias so materially promoted the happiness of the slaves. To You, our bonded Fellow Beings, wlm like all men, ate placed by the Allwise Providence in a more or less limited situation, 1 feel it a duty incumbent on me, earnestly and sincerely to advise to follow your hitherto pursued peaceful and orderly conduct, which has made you worthy of the solicitude and benevolence of our lieloved Sovereign, as good order, industry and obedience to your masters are the only means by which any further ameliorations in your condition may be obtained.

Cum. E. Kajik. Proclamation ! UNDER protection of Divine Providence, and in obedience to the command of our most gracious Sovereign, 1 am once more afforded the pleasure of being placed among you, my fellow subjects, in order to exert myself sincerely, and candidly to preserve peace and tranquility in His Majesty's Colonies, and promote the pros|»erity thereof. This object I am well aware cannot be obtained, but by your mutual assistance and your confidence in my measures, and from my experience during the number of years 1 have been intrusted with the administration of this Island, 1 feel confident 1 shall want neither. In regard to owners of slaves and their agents, it is scarcely necessary for me to recommend a continuance of the humane and prudent conduct towards those under their charge, which of late years, at the same time it conferred honor on the masters, has so materially promoted the happiness of the slaves. To You, our bonded Fellow Beings, who like all men, are placed by the A II wise Providence in a more or less limited situation, 1 feel it a duty incumbent on me, earnestly and sincerely to advise to follow your hitherto pursued peaceful and orderly conduct, which has made you worthy of the solicitude and benevolence of our beloved Sovereign, as good order, industry and obedience to your masters are the only means by which any further ameliorations in your ooudiliou may bo obtained
No. 219. Regierings Avis, TORSDAGEN den Me FEBRUARIl 1835.

It is the pleasure of Our Most Gracious King, that only a gradual improvement conjunctively with your masters co-operation, shall pave the way for you to such advantages as a Christian like conduct with order and industry may render you worthy and capable of enjoying. After my best wishes for the welfare and happiness of all and every individual in the Colonies, I have only to add the assurance, that, keeping in view the interest and prosperity of these Islands, I shall ever righteously and conscientiously employ my efforts with energy and impartiality to the protection of all and every His Majesty's Loyal Subjects, without distinction in regard either to persons or their stations in these Colonies GOD SA VE THE KING ! Government General of the Danish Westindia Islands, St. Croix, the 2d February, 1835 P. c. SCUOLTtN.

Morrison, of the Royal Navy, has published a most interesting work upon this magnificent phenomenon, which is expected to he seen in the course of the next year, 1835, between the months of May and August, in the constellation of Ursa Major. Lieutenant Morrison States that it will he far more splendid than the one of 1811: some writers affirm that it will afford a degree of " light equal to a lull moon, that its tail will extend over forty degrees," and when the head ol the comet readies the meridian, its tail will sweep the horizon. The author contends that the electric and attractive powers of the comet will have very serious eflects upon our atmosphere, in producing inundations, earthquakes, orins, tempests, volcanic eruptions, s and epidemic diseases. In support of this þÿ theory, he refers to the different appearances ol tiiis comet for the last six hundred years þÿ showing that in the comet years these phenomena prevailed to a great extent. þÿ The warmth of last winter and the violent winds, as well as the great heat of the late summer, are attributed to the approach of the Comet. The author says : þÿ " Relying on the correctness of our principle of comuietry influence, we venture to predict that the summer of 1835 will he remarked for intense heat, which may be expected to destroy the harvest in some parts of the world; That year will be noted for earthquakes and volcanoes, and other similar phenomena. þÿ The end of 1835, or early in 1830,

may be expected to he remarkable for some one or more very extensive earthquakes. þÿ The winters of 1830 or 1837, will bring a frost sucli as has not been equalled for at least twenty years. The parts of the earth which, we anticipate will suffer most, are those situated to the north of Asia, and some parts of the southern hemisphere, such as China. But those parts which arc in the vicinity of volcanoes, such as Italy, Dalmatia, &c., arc of course, always subject to the electrical phenomena of earthquakes, because the frequent internal changes which the combustion continually in action creates, must necessarily produce a derangement of electricity. And if, while the cornet is near the earth, overcharged with electricity, as at the same time it was in perihelion in 1456, there be any internal cavity of the earth, by which combustion of sulphur, &c., is deficient of that fluid, it will rush into the earth at that spot. This we take to have been the case, at that period, near Naples, when the sudden renting of the earth destroyed forty thousand human beings.

In June, 1833, a miller received a sahrccut at a public house, which completelv amputated his right ear. Before lie left t liehouse he picked up the ear from the grot nd, and put it into his pocket; this was in the evening. Early in the following morning lie went to a surgeon and showed him the ear, now cold and somewhat crushed. The surgeon washed the ear in spirits and water, and made a new edge to the wound of the which the man still possessed, and to that part of the ear which he had lost. After accurately fitting the parts, he kept them together by four stitches, and dressed them with adhesive plasters, compresses, and an appropiate bandage. The day alter some ot the dressings were removed, in order to make sure that the parts were in contact ; the point of union was then observed to be red : the patient was feverish, and had thirst and head-ache. In eights days these symptoms disappeared, and the helix began to assume its vital warmth ; the lobular extremity united the first ; the other parts suppurated, and granulations appeared on the cartilages. In a little more than a month the cure was complete ; the patient's right ear was almost in the same condition as the left, and all that was remarked was an elliptic linear cicatrix at the point ol union. þÿ Medical and Surgical Journal.

UNDER protection of Divine Providence, and in obedience to the command of our most gracious Sovereign, 1 am once more afforded the pleasure ot being placed among you, my fellow subjects, in order to exert myself sincerely, and candidly to preserve peace and tranquility in His Majesty's Colonies, and promote the prosperity thereof. This object I am well aware cannot be obtained, but by your mutual assistance and your confidence in my measures, and from my experience during the number of years I have been intrusted with the administration of this Island, I feel confident 1 shall want neither. In regard to owners of slaves and their agents, it is scarcely necessary for me to recommend a continuance of the humane and prudent conduct towards those under their charge, w hich of late years, at the same time it conferred honor on the masters, has so materially promoted the happiness of the slaves. To You, our bonded Fellow Beings, who like all men, are plaeed by the Allwise Providence in a more or less limited situation, I leel it a duty incumbent on me, earnestly and sincerely to advise to follow your hitherto pursued peaceful and orderly conduct, which has made you worthy of the solicitude and benevolence of our beloved Sovereign, as good order, industry and obedience to your masters are the only means by which any further ameliorations in your condition may be obtained. It is the pleasure of Our Most Gracious King, that only a gradual improvement conjunctively with your masters co-operation,
shall pave the way lor you to such advan-

A Portuguese Corvette, anchored at Gibraltar on the Kith ult., from Italy, with the Prince of I.euchtenburg on board, who was ori his way to Lisbon to espouse the Queen of Portugal. The young Queen of Portugal was married to the Duke of Leuchtenburg by proxy on the 1st instant, at Lisbon. 1. on don, Dec. 8. þÿ We have just received an express, which- left Falmouth at five o'clock yesterday morning. Tfie time is too short for us to enter into all the details of our correspondence from Lisbon, brought by the Confiance steamer, which left that city on the 2d instant, in the afternoon ; but the summary of the chief part of the information is as follows : þÿ The 1st instant being a grand day for the Portuguese nation, in as much as it is the celebration of the accession of the House of Braganza to the Throne, was rendered uncommonly interesting and important this time, by the marriage of the young Queen (by proxy) to the Prince of Leuchtenburg, an event which may be considered as tending to the consolidation of the great work of the deceased lamented Emperor Don Pedro, more especially as it has taken place with a unanimity rarely witnessed, þÿ as not only the ( hamhers hut the municiplities and the people at large have all felt the necessity of it to put an end to any factious hopes and to fix firmly the constitution of the country. Spain. þÿ I he report that the Carlists had gained a victory over the Queen's troops on the 27th and 28th ult. is confirmed. It is

stated that 2000 of the Queen's troops were killed, and that the prisoners were 1000 in number, among whom were General O'Dovle, his brother, and several other officers of rank. The revolting, and cold-blooded murders committed, in retaliation, by both parties, still continue to disgrace them. General O'Doyle and his officers were shot after the day of buttle. Zumalacarreguy, the hero of the victory, has been elevated by Don Carlos to the rank of Grand Cross of the Order of St. Ferdinand. Mina's appearance in the North of Spain has given fresh courage to the Queen's troops. He is organizing new corps, and carrying forward his operations with great vigour. The Procuradores have agreed to the amendments of the Proceres on the Finance question Alina has ordered every man in the Provinces to enrol himself as a National Guard, or quit the Country in 48 hours. Portugal. þÿ The Cortes have passed a law excluding Don Miguel and his descendants, forever, from the succession to the Portuguese Throne. Should they enter the Portuguese dominions, they are immediately to be shot. Admiral Napier has retired as Portuguese Admiral, with £r>00 a-year, as half pay. The Duchess de Herri has met Don Carlos in Genoa, doubtless by agreement, to consult as to the grand blow, w hich, according to the legitimate Journals, is about to be struck for the restoration of the three Pretenders to their respective thrones of France, Portugal, and Spain.

Lord Lowther is, it is said, to succeed Sir John Hobhouse as Fiist Commissioner of the Woods and Forests, and the Earl of Haddington to succeed Mr. Spring Rice at the Colonial-office. It is also said that Mr. Sergeant Pennefether is to be Attorney-General and Mr. Jackson Solicitor-General for Ireland, and that Sir William Gosset is likely to remain in his present situation. Who will be the new Lord Lieutenant is yet undetermined. It is rumoured that Sir Charles Wetherell is to be Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. Sir Charles is a most honest and consistent Tory and high Churchman. The Colonial Department has been offered to the Earl of Haddington, and the Woods and Forests to Lord I.owther. No answer has yet been received from either. The Standard says that the Earl de Grey will be first Lord of the Admiralty, in the room of the Earl of Aberdeen, who will be Secretary of State for the Colonial Department.. Mr. Pemberton has declined the Solicitor Generalship ; an offer of which will be made, without delay, to Mr. Follett. The Marquess Wellesley has been recalled ; and the administration of affairs in Ireland confided, pro tempore , to three Lord Justices, as usual upon the occasional suspension of the Vice-regal dignity. The Lords Justices are þÿ the Lord Primate, the Commander of the Forces, and the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench. þÿ John Bull. We are sorry to announce that the Queen is indisposed, arising from a severe cold.

Prussia. þÿ The Emperor of Russia, the Duke of Nassau, and the Prince of Orange, have all been visiting the King of Prussia at

Berlin. The continental journals declare that the meeting had no connexion with politics, and was merely a family party. The Royal re-union, however, it must be allowed, was singularly-timed, if politics had nothing to do with it.

In a valley near Nazareth, is a fountain which bears the name of the Virgin Mary, and where the women are seen passing to and fro with pitchers on their heads as in days of old. It is justly remarked that, if there lie a spot throughout the Holy Land which was more particularly honoured by the presence of Mary, we may consider this to be the place; because the situation of a copious spring is not liable to change, and because the custom of repairing thif.icr to draw water has been continued among the females of Nazareth from the earliest period of its history. þÿ Findon's Landscape Illustrations of the Bible.

Some time since, a Welch jury acquitted a prisoner charged with a capital offence, who pleaded guilty ; when the judge having asked them on what grounds they returned such a verdict, the foreman answered, " because my lord, the prisoner has been a notorious liar since he was able to speak, and therefore we do not believe a word he says." Shortly after, the late Baron Richards was proceeding in his carriage through Wales, accompanied by a friend, when they observed a hare hard pressed by a brace ol greyhounds and in great danger, on perceiving which, the Baron exclaimed, "alas! poor puss, there is nothing but a Welch jury can save you."

THE HUMAN HAND. There is inconsistency, and something of the child's propensities, still in mankind. A piece of mechanism, as a watch, a barometer, or a dial, will fix attention ; a man will take journeys to see an engine stamp a coin, or turn a block ; yet the organs through which he has a thousand sources of enjoyment, and which are, in themselves, more exquisite in design and more curious, both in contrivance) and in mechanism, do not enter his thoughts; if he admire a living action, his admiration will, probably, be more excited, by what is uncommon and monstrous, than by what is natural and perfectly adjusted to its office þÿ by the elephant's trunk, than by the human hand. This does not arise from an unwillinjjness to contemplate the superiority or dignity of our own nature, nor from an incapacity of admiring the adaptation of parts. It is the effect ol habit. The human hand is so beautifully formed, every effort of the will is answered so instantly, as if the hand itself were the seat ol that will, that the very perfection of the instrument makes us insensible to its use; we use it as we draw our breath, unconsciously, we have lost all recollection of the feeble and ill-directed efforts of its first exercise, by which it has been perfected, and we are insensible of the advantages we derive from it. The armed extremities of a variety of animals, give them great advantages ; but if man possessed any similar provisions, he would forfeit his sovereignty over all. As

Galen long since observed, " did man possess" the natural armour of the brutes, he would no longer work as an artificer, nor protect himself with a breast-plate, nor fashion a sword or spear, nor invent a bridle to mount a horse, and hunt the lion. Neither could he follow the arts of peace, construct the pipe and lyre, erect houses, inscribe laws, ana through letters and the ingenuity of the hand, converse with the sages of aniiquity." þÿ Sir Charles Bells Bridgwater Treatise.

sir robert peel. Sir Robert Peel is the eldest son of the late Baronet, by his tust wife, the daughter of his partner, Air. Yates, and was born the 5th February, I7SS. He commenced his education at Harrow, where he displayed uncommon aptitude and ability, uniting ready tj|l<-nt with steady application. Lord Byron, his contemporary, savs of him, " Peel, the orator, and statesman, that was, or is, or is to be, was my form-fellow, and we were both at the top of our remove, n public school phrase. We were on good terms, but his brother was my intimate friend. There were always great hopes of Peel amongst us all, master and scholars, and he has not disappointed us. As a scnolar he was greatly inv superior; as a declaimer and actor 1 was reckoned at least his equal. Asa school-bov, out of school. I was always in scrapes, and lie never: and in school he always knew his T-son, and I arely." In due time Mr. Peel entered tin I niversity ot < 'xford, as a commoner of Christchurch. In 1-soy lie took his seat as a member for Cashol. and early in INK) seconded the address ot thanks to the Throne. I luring the same year he was made Under-Secretary ot State; and in September, 1812, was appointed Chief Secretary for Ireland. It is generally supposed that from the period of Ids leaving Oxford he was marked out for the honour of representing the University in Parliament, whenever a vacancy should occur This look place on the elevation of Mr. Abbott, Speaker of the House of Commons, to

the peerage, in Itsi 7, when Mr. J'eel was elected to succeed him. In 1822 he succeeded Viscount Sidmonth as Secretary of State for the Home Dot, artmen t, and, with a short interval only, held that high office eight years. In 1826 lie commenced his most important measures, those for the improvement of the criminal code. On the appointment of i\Jr. Canning as Premier he resigned, hut returned to office under the Duke of Wellington. The change in his opinions on the Catholic question led to the resignation of his seat at Oxford ; he accepted the Chiltern Hundreds, and stood at the ensuing election, but unsuccessful! v. þÿ Tn the right lion, baronet's public avowal of political opinion to the electors of Tarn worth, in 1 832, he said, "That he had never been the decided supporter of any hand of partisans, but had always thought it much Letter to look steadily at the peculiar circumstances of the times in which they lived, and if necessities were so pressing as to demand it, there was no dishonour nor discredit :ri relinquishing opinions or measures, and adopting mhers more suited to the altered stale of the country. For this course of proceeding he had been censured by opposite parties, by those who upon all occasions thought that no changes were required, as well as by those who, in his opinion, were the advocates of too violent and sudden innovations. That middle course, however, he would continue to pursue ; he la id it to he impossible for any statesman to adopt one fixed line of policy under all circum-
stances, and the only question with when he departed from that line should he, am I actuated by any interested or sinister motive? þÿ

On the demise of his father, in 1830, he succeeded to the Baronetcy, and almost the largest private fortune of any commoner in England. In 1820 Sir Robert married his present amiable and accomplished lady, a daughter of the late Gen. Sir John Floyd, Bart., by whom he has a family of seven children. þÿ St. James's Chronicle.

MY SISTER. (A lesson for Children.) One morning in my early lite. I remember to have been playing with a younger sister not then three years old. It was one ot those bright mornings in spring, that bring joy and life to the heart, and diffuse gladness and animation through all the tribes of living creatures. Our feelings were in perfect harmony with the universal gladness of nature. Even now 1 seem to hear the merry laugh of my little sister, as she followed me through the winding alleys of the garden, her cheek sutlused with the glow of health and animation, and her waving hair floating in the wind. She was an only sister, the sole companion ol all my childish sports. We were constantly together; and my young heart went out to hers, with all the affection, all the fondness, of which childhood is capable. Nothing afforded me enjoyment, in which she did not participate; no amusement was sought, which we cuulu no! snare together. 'I ! it morning we had prolonged our play ti'l near the hour of breakfast, with undiminisln i ardor, when at some slight provocation my impetuous nature broke forth, and in my anger, / struck my little sister a blow with inv hand. She turned to inc an appealing look, and the large tears came into her þÿ eyes. Her heart was too full to allow her to speak, and shame made rue silent. At that moment the breakfast bell announced us away, and we returned to the house, without exchanging a word. The exeitcnient of the play was over, and as she sat beside my mother at

breakfast, I perceived by occasional stolen glances at her, that she was pale and sad. A tear seemed ready to start in her eye, which her little self-possession could scarcely repress. Il was only when my mother inquired if she was ill, that she drank her coflee, and endeavored to eat. I was ashamed and grieved ; and inwardly resolved to embrace the first opportunity when we were alone, to throw my arms around her neck and entreat her forgiveness. When breakfast was ended, my mother retired with her into her own room, directing me in the mean time to sit down to my lesson. I seated myself by the window, and ran over my lesson, hut did not learn it. My thoughts were perpetually recurring to the scene in the garden, and at table. It was long before my mother returned, and when she did, it was with an agitated look, and hurried step, to tell mo that, poor Ellen was very ill. I asked eagerly if I might go to her, hut was not permitted, lest I should disturb her. A physician was called, and every means used for her recovery, hut to no purpose. The disease, which was in her head, constantly increased in violence, and she became delirious. It

ji/rrs. was not until evening that i was permitted to see her. She was a little recovered from the severity of her pain, and lay with her eyes opened, and her little hand resting ori the pillow beneath her head. How I longed to tell her the sorrow I felt for my unkindness to her in the morning, and how much I had suffered for it during the day. But 1 was forbidden to speak to her, and was soon taken out of the room. During that night, and the day following, she continued to grow worse. I saw her several times, but she was always insensible of my presence. ( >nce indeed, she showed some signs of consciousness, and asked for me, but immediately relapsed into her former state. On the morning of the third day, I rose at an early hour, and repaired to the sick room. My mother was sitting by the bed. as I entered, she drew me to her, and for some time was silent, while the tears flowed fast down her face. I first learned that my sweet sister was dead, as her mother drew aside the curtain that concealed her from me. I felt as though my heart would break. The remembrance of her affection for me, and my last unkind deed, revived in my mind ; and burying my face in the folds of the curtain, I wept long and bitterly. I saw her laid in the coffin, and lowered into the grave. 1 almost wished to lie down there with her, if so 1 might see once more her smile, and hear my forgivness pronounced in her sweet voice.

His Britannic Majesty's Packet Lyra, Captain St. John, arrived here yesterday afternoon, with the second November Mails. The. dates reach to the 22 d, from Falmouth, and confirm the report of the Duke, oj Wellington as Premier, in consequence of Lord Melbourne's resignation. A change in the French ministry has also taken place, and Marshal Mortier, I'ukc of Treuiso, is appointed head minister.

oil Thursday Evening, J past seven. In the hands of the Duke of Wellington is the whole government of the country. Yesterday a gentleman from each of the government olfices waited on the Duke at the Home otlice with such documents as required his Grace's signature. No appointments to the ministry have yet been announced, but it is said that to-morrow commissioners will be appointed without salary, to perform certain duties at the Treasury, until the linal arrangements are made. These commissioners, it is understood, will not be members of Parliament, that no re-election may be rendered necessary. Lord Justices are to be appointed for Ireland. The Great Seal, which Lord

Brougham will resign to-morrow is to be put in commission; the Lord Chief Baron (f.yndhurst,) Mr. Justice Bosanquet, and one of the Judges of the Court of King's Bench are to be the Commissioners. To-day his majesty held a Council at St. James's palace, which was attended by the Duke of Wellington, Lords Cowley, Maryborough, Rosslvn, Ellenborough, Jersey, the Speaker of the House of Commons, Sir H. llardinge, and Mr. c.oulburn. At this Council it was resolved that Parliament should be further prorogued until the first week in February, when the houses will meet for the despatch of business. The Duke of Devonshire had an audience of his majesty, and resigned the key of his office as Lord Chamberlain of the Household ; and the Earl of Derby was sworn in Lord Lieutenant of the county of Lancaster, in the place of his late father. His majesty holds another council to-morrow, when it is expected that several members of the new administration will be sworn in.

The Paris papers of Sunday announce the re-construction of the Doctrinaire Cabinet, with Marshal Mortier, Duke ofTreviso, at its head. On Saturday morning Louis Philippe sent for his old ministers. He Uigny, Thiers, Guizot, and Duchatel, who immediately obeyed the summons ; and the Duke of Treviso followed shortly after, and accepted the office of Minister of War and President of the Council. M.JJcrnard resumes his station as Aid-de-camp to the King ; Admiral Jacob resumes the Marine Department, and M. Persil, who has not resigned, remains m statu quo as Minister of Justice. The Thkee Days Fkench þÿMinistry. The new ministry born on Monday, expired on Thursday. Messrs. Pussy, Teste, Bassano, Bernard, and Charles Dupin, have given in their resignations ; which were immediately accepted. The insisting of some of the Cabinet, that the 25 millions of indemnity to the Americans should become a ministerial question in the Chamber, is considered by some as the immediate cause. City, Four o'clock. þÿ The letters from Paris of Monday's date, received this morning, bring the prices of the French and other funds in the market lower, in consequence of the Ministerial changes having become known. At about 25 minutes before 9 o'clock on Tuesday morning last, the inhabitants of St. George's, were thrown into great consternation, by oik; of the severest shocks of earthquake which have been for some time felt here, and which continued without intermission for about 30 seconds. It was preceded
No. 210. Regierings Avis. MANDAGEN den 5 te JANUARII 1835.

by a loud subterranean noise similar to the roaring of distant winds and waves, and the shock vvas most violent at its commencement ; þÿ it gradually subsided in violence until a few seconds before its termination, when the vibration or rather undulation of the earth, proceeding from S. W. to N. E., became a second time alarmingly violent. It is generally considered that the shock was more severe than any experienced here since September, 1825. We have heard of no damage done to any of the buildings in town ; but it is said that slight fissures have shewn themselves in consequence in one or two dwelling houses about the north end of the Island. It is generally remarked, and we believe, correctly, that the violence and repetitions of those awful visitations have, of late years, gained strength, and been more frequent. We have heard it asserted that on Tuesday morning the bells in the steeple of our Church were rung by the violence of the motion, but we have no recollection of hearing them. The following paragraph from The St. Vincent Gazette, by Authority, of the 27 th instant, w ill shew our readers that the earthquake was also felt in that Island : þÿ The severest shock of Earthquake ever felt in this Island, we believe, occurred on Tuesday morning last, at about 50 minutes after eight o'clock. The direction was from South to North, and the duration in the whole about eight or ten seconds. The .-hock was preceded by a rumbling noise, and was at the commencement slight ; but it became so vio-

lent towards the end, that had it continued a few seconds longer it is the general belief that most of the houses in town would have been destroyed. Several chimnies in the country were thrown down, and several houses in town slightly injured. We have been also informed that the church bells were lung by the shock. The morning was fair, although heavy rains had fallen during the night ; and it is probably, to a long spell of dry weather, succeeded by these rains, that the Earthquake is fairly to be attributed; but we fear, from its direction, that the shock has been destructive in the southern settlements.

With a hop, step, and a jump, as it were ; for instance, when friends assemble, on some grand and solemn occasion, at some public, gorgeous festival, to enjoy the " feast of reason and the How of soul," they have three courses, of course ; the cloth is drawn, and Non nobis Domine" chaunted by three " voices, the chairman rises, and with due emphasis, energy, and discretion, gives " Church and King." How is it received why with three to be sure, or rather three times three, duly vociferated at succession threes, a of roared out by some stentorian voice, hip, þÿ hip, hip, again, again, again, now, now, þÿ þÿ now, þÿ &c. (fcc. &c. þÿ The schoolmasters might well call the liule of Three, " the golden rule," tor it works every thing. Great Britain is divided into three, England, Ireland, and Scotland. The Constitution is tripartite too, King, Cords, and Commons. Julius Caesar begins his Commentaries, "Gallia est omnis divisa in partes Ires." Number three seems to affect all orders and degrees of men þÿ the banker does not pay his bill when it is due, but takes three day's grace. How do the cavalry turn about? by threes. How do the infantry stand in line ? three deep. When a soldier presents arms he must do it in three motions þÿ rattle, slap, bang. When he attacks his enemy three again þÿ ready, present, fire. What do you tell a quarrelsome, troublesome lellow to beware of þÿ the

third time to be sure ; he may do what he likes once or twice, but let him take care of number three. Three won't let the poor school boys alone : there are three degrees of comparison, three concords in grammar, which the poor fellows often think don't agree with them at all, but on the contrary. Three terms in a proposition þÿ three propositions in a syllogism ; and, by the bye, this is the reason, I suppose, people are said to jump to a conclusion, and three angles to a triangle,

and what lots of things we do by triangles. Three was every thing with the witches ; " Thrice the brinded cat has mew'd," says Shakspeare ; three was a quorum of these worthies (witches I mean, not cats,) " When shall we three meet again?" for business, no doubt. Nobody can be married without the presence ot three, the lady, the gentleman, anu the parson ; and then they must have been asked three times. There should be three parts in every oration þÿ a beginning, middle and end ; though in some modern speeches it would strangely puzzle one to find where these points exactly are, especially the last. Three learned professions þÿ Three graces þÿ Three times three muses þÿ a pretty little jingling, harmonious equilateral triangle. What would the mayor's coachman be, Without his hut cocked up in three ? Why, Mr. Printer, þÿ No-bo-dy. Three stares me in the face, look where 1 will ; I cannot even turn to the fire, but I find the grate under the guard of three þÿ poker, shovel, and tongs A man cannot come into the world, with any sense of decency, without the presence of three þÿ the mother, the doctor, and the nurse; and lie cannot go out of it again with any proper decorum, without the professional assistance of three þÿ the doctor, the undertaker, and the parson. Then the freemasons again þÿ three has a mighty influence with them, as any one may convince himself of by listening when they are at their þÿrevels clap ! clap! clap! their very knockers on their doors arc triangles ! Falstaff says there are but three

good men unhanged in England; talking of Falstafl", three goes to the play, and divides all the audience into three þÿ boxes, pit, and gallery. To cut the matter short, number three seems to be every where, and to meddle with every body. Even if this ever gets into print, three must be þÿconcerned it will be between you, and I, and the post. But having written down three sides of mv paper, it is high time I should take my leave, which shall do in three words þÿ one two three þÿ þÿ AND AWAY.'

In the prison of the Fort du Ha, Bordeaux , there is confined a man of the name of Jacques Dubu isson, who was sentenced in the year 1818 to 20 years' imprisonment for the murder, without premeditation, of his father. At the time this man was tried for the offence he was only 14 years of age, hut was a/ways of violent passions and temperament, and it was after a violent quarrel with his father that he stabbed him and injliited a mortal wound ; but the Court, taking into consideration his ' "der age, sentenced him to 20 years of solitary imprisonment in the gloomy prison of the Fort du Ha, instead of inflicting the capital punishment. This man was of good family. At his entrance into the prison he was a stout active youth, but in the course of the first 12 months' imprisonment, he dwindled au ay almost to a shadow. þÿ lie for some time bore his situation with calmness, and it was apparently not until he had been in prison for some considerable period of time that the horror of his sentence broke upon, him. His conduct became then so outrageous that it was found necessary to confine him. and for several weeks he wore a strait-waistcoat, and was attended by a keeper. W hen he recovered from Itis paroxysm, he became quite an altered being. His eyes were continually fixed in vacancy, and although he obtained a remission of his sentence so far as to be allowed occasionally to have intercourse with his fellow prisoners, yet he took no advantage of it, and seldom or never uttered a word, but kept walk-

ing about the prison yard with every appearance of a maniac. After he had been imprisoned ten years, his hair was partly turned grey, and he had all the appearance of an idiot, lie has ever since become more arid more emaciated, and he has now undergone 18 years of his sentence, and although now only 32 years of age, he appears like a man of 50, and is quite childish At the expiration of the term o f his sentence, he will, in all probability, be placed in some receptacle for idiots, as he has lost all sense and recollection of the world and every thing connected with it, and is quite incapable of taking any care of himself, lie, does not appear to have the least conception of any thing beyond the prison u al/s, or ant. desire to be at liberty. þÿ Gazette de$ 'i'libwiuax

TOMB OF COLUMBUS. The relics of Columbus þÿ "a number of bones and a quantity of mould, evidently the remains of a human body" þÿ have rested for the hist eight and thirty years in the cathedral of Havannah, the capital of Cuba. Every voyager who touches at the Island, is anxious to make a devotional pilgrimage to this me- morial of the illustrious mariner, " who first had the judgment to divine, and the intrepidity to brave, the mysteries of this perilous deep (the Atlantic); and who, by his hardy genius, his inflexible constancy, and his heroic courage, brought the ends of the earth into communication with each other." Fireside travellers hold, propoitionally, in esteem every record of the troubled life and the memorable obsequies of Columbus. By turning to Washington Irving's Life of Columbus , we find appended several particulars of his obsequies. Columbus died at Valladolid, in Spain, with great resignation, on the 20th of April 160(3. He was surrounded words were ; " In mantis tuas Dominc ! coin- by a few devotional friends, and ins last mendo spiritum mcum" " Into thy hands, U Lord! 1 commend my spirit." " The body of Columbus was deposited in the convent of St. Francisco, and bis obsequies were celebrated with funeral pomp in the parochial church of Santa Marie de la Antiqua, in Valladolid. llis remains were transported in 1513, to the Carthusian convent of Las Cuevas, at Seville, and deposited in the chapel of Santa Christo. In the year 153(5, they were removed to Hispaniola, and

interred by the side of the grand altar of the city of San Domingo. But even here they did not rest in quiet. On the cession of Hispaniola to the French iu 1795, it was determined by the Spaniards to bear them ylf to the Island of Cuba, .as precious relics, con- »

Accordingly, on the 20th of December, 1795, in the presence of an august assemblage of all the dignitaries of the church, and the civil and military officers, the vault was opened beside the high altar ol the cathedral : within were found the fragments of a leaden coffin, a number of bones, and a quantity of mould evidently the remains of a human body. These were carefully collected, and put into a case of gilded lead, secured by an iron lock ; the case was enclosed in a coffin covered with black velvet, and the whole placed in a temporary mausoleum. On the following day, there was another grand eonvocation at the cathedral the vigils and masses for the dead were chanted, and a funeral sermon was preached by the archbishop. After these solemn ceremonials in the cathedral, the coffin was transported to the ship attended by a grand civil, religious, and military procession. The banners were covered with crape ; there were chants, and responses, and discharges of artillery ; and the most distinguished persons of the several orders took turns to support the coffin. " The reception of the body at Havannah was equally august. There was a splendid procession of bouts to conduct it from the ship to the shore. On passing the vessels of war in the harbour, they all paid the honors due to an admiral and captain-general of the navy. Oil arriving at the mole the remains were met by the governor of the island, accompanied by the generals of the military

stall. They were then conveyed in the utmost pomp, to the cathedral. Masses and the solemn ceremonies ol the dead were performed by the bishop, and the mortal remains of Columbus were deposited in the wall, on the right side of the grand altar where tiicy still remain."

Captain T. E. Alexander, who travelled sixteen thousand miles by flood, and field, in the space of a twelvemonth, lias described bis visit to the tomb of Columbus in four of the most entertaining pages ot his journal, (tn the morning after bis arrival in llavannah he, says : " I rose at an early hour, and hastened to the tomb ot Columbus. The cathedral in which his precious remains are deposited ooeuptes one side ol a small square. The exterior of the building is of massive stone, of no particular order of architecture ; its gable rises hi a pyramidal shape; on the ajiex is a cross, and on cither side are towers; pillars adorn the building, and behind these, hired assassins frequently lurk. 1 passed into the body of the church, and was struck with its grandeur and simplicity. The roof was arched and very lofty, and Saxon arches enclosed the aisles. The whole was tastefully painted in imitation of grey marble, and there were none of the gaudy colours and tinsel decorations, which arc too often met with in Catholic churches. " Exquisite paintings were disposed here and there round the wails; one was the announcement to Sarah, by the angel, of her miraculous conception ; another, out Saviour conversing with the woman of Samaria at the well ; whilst in the same were representations of Moses, the Prophets, and the Evangelists. The principal altar, at the upper end, was chastely and richly ornamented. Within the railing was a mosaic floor of marble, and the seats of the dignitaries were highly carved.

Looking to the left, I saw a slab of white marble let into the wall ; this was the monument of Columbus, and as there was only a single priest in the cathedral, we obtained' his permission to approach the tomb. " I was under the influence of no ordinary sensations on finding myself in so interesting a situation. I stood beside the mouldering bones of the most intrepid mariner who ever Jived. He must be dull and insensible, indeed, who could contemplate the final resting place of the great Colon, without being powerfully affected, and without sympathizing deeply in the sorrows and sufferings of his latter days. " The efligy of Columbus is in mezzo relievo, and represents him with a long visage,

prominent lirows and moustaches ; round his neck is a straight nose, curled hair, full eye double ruff, and his wrist is similarly ornamented. His body is cased in armour to the waist ; a scarf is thrown across the breast, ami the fore finger of the right hand points to America on a globe. Naval emblems are helow the half length of 'the worthy and adventurous General of the seas,' consisting of a cannon, rudder, anchor, oar, quadrant, compass, sand-glass, &e., and in the midst of these, the follow ing inscription : þÿ " Restos e Imager del Grande Colon, Mil siglos durud guardados in la urna, Y in remembranza de vuestra nacion

Remains and Image of the Great Columbus, A thousand ages continue preserved in the urn , And in the remembrance of our nation ! " The enthusiastic biographer of Columbus, YV ashington Irving, had been most kind to mo in giving me many introductions to his friends in America, and 1 was anxious to obtain some ' let the hand of the man whoever attempts to relic from the tomb to present to him. But mutilate or efface it be withered.' i would not have done it for the wealth of Potosi, hut 1 was fortunate enough to observe a small fragment of wood which lay under the slab, but in no way connected with it, and seizing it with the avidity of an antiquary, 1 bore it oil' in triumph." Washington Irving adds to the passage altouching conclusion: " it is with deep satis- ready quoted, the þÿ following eloquent and laction that the author is able to close iiis history with the account of a ceremonial so noble and affecting, and so honorable t< > the Spanish Nation When we read of the remains of Columbus thus conveyed from the port of San Domingo, after an interval of near three hundred years, as sacred national relics, with civil and military pomp, and high religious ceremonial, we cannot but reflect that it was from this very port lie was carried off, load' d with ignominious chains, blasted, apparent it iti fame and fortune, and taunted by the revilings ol the rabble : sucli honors, it is true, are nothing to the dead, nor can they alone to the heart, now dust and ashes, for all the wrongs

and sorrows it may have suffered ; hut they speak volumes of comfort to the illustrious, yet slandered and persecuted living, encouraging them bravely to bear with present injuries, by shewing them how true merit outlives all calumny, and receives its glorious reward in the admiration of after ages."

It was the custom of Sir Humphrey Davy annually to visit Ballyshanuon, Ireland, merely to enjoy the fine fishing for which the river is so celebrated þÿ a sport of which lie was t scessivoh fond. Having after many fruitless attempts, owing to the inapplicability of his flies (tor lie was an excellent fislicr,) succeeded in landing a fine salmon, tie called to Ins servant, and desired him to take it to his hotel. John reluctantly obeyed, for having no basket, ho did not much relish conveying the fish in his hand. He hud gone hut a very short distance indeed from him cf the safety lamp notoriety, when he oflered sixpence to any one to do the business for him. Sir Humphrey hearing htm, bawled out " I'll take your money, Sir." John apologized, begged pardon, and stammered an excuse. " No, no," says 1hc master, "give me the sixpence, John, I insist on it;" and he took the fish from him, and walked w ith it in his hand through the street, the servant bowing and apologizing t he whole way, in momentary expectation ofheing dismissed. In this however, the philosopher agreeably disappointed him ; he did not discharge him, but contented himself with depriving him of the sixpence, and lecturing hint freely on the folly of such preposterous conduct in a waiting man.

DISMISSAL OF FORI) MELBOURNE AND HIS COLLEARUES. The death of F.ail Spencer and the consequent succession of Lord Althorp to the title of his venerable father, whereby he was removed from the Mouse of Commons, as wc slated last week, rendered some arrangements

og UdGIVET af It I char i) IIatchett. in his majesty's councils necessary. To take his majesty's instructions on tins important subject, Lord Melbourne on Thursday last proceeded to Brighton, where he had an interview with the King, by whom, of course, he was very courteously received. The result, however, of the noble lord's conference with the King was, that his majesty no longer required the services of Lord Melbourne and his colleagues þÿ an intimation which his lordship communicated to the rest of the cabinet ministers on his return to town on Friday. þÿ This intelligence was made public on Saturday morning, accompanied by the information that the new cabinet would he composed of the Duke of Wellington and those persons who coincided with Ins Grace in political opinion þÿ expectedly that a strong sensation was the consequence. Men stood astounded at the change on which his majesty hud determined þÿ a change implying an opposite course of policy hi conducting the affairs of the nation to that which had been pursued by the lute ministry as well as that of Furl Grey, which his majesty had so warmly supported, and all wondered how such a change had been produced in the royal mind. !So extraordinary did the affair seem, that at first the public would not give credence to the statement. They were sure there must he some " mistake." In the course of a few hours, however, it was made known that the Duke of Wellington had been sent for by majesty, his with whom his Grace dined on Saturday evening, and it was speedily announced that an

arrangement had been made for the return of the noble Duke and his friends to power, and that the King would on Monday hold a court, to accept the seals of office lrom Lord Melbourne and his colleagues. By this intelligence men's minds were raised to a degree of excitement that it is impossible to describe. The Tories, as a matter of course, were delighted þÿ the Reformers were equally astonished, and immediately took those steps which they deemed prudent in such a crisis. The King and Queen arrived in town at half-past one o'clock on Monday afternoon from the Pavilion at Brighton, and at two o'clock his majesty held a Court. '1 he Duke of Wellington and Lord I.yndhurst had audiences of the King. His majesty then gave audiences to the following members ol Viscount Melbourne's administration on their retirement from office, viz: þÿ Lord Brougham (Lord Chancellor,) Viscount Melbourne (First Lord of the Treasury,) the Marquis of Lansdown (Lord President of the Council,) the Karl of Mulgrave (Lord I'rivy Seal,) Viscount Duncannon, Viscount 1'almerston, and Mr. Spring Rice, (Secretary of Stale for the Home, Foreign, and Colonial Departments,) Lord Auckland (First Lord of the Admiralty,) the Right Hon. Chns. Grant (President of the Board of Control,) Lord Holland (Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancas- '

Ionor a yce. þÿ Survey our faults, our errors, our vices þÿ fearful and fertile field, þÿ trace them to their causes, all those causes resolve themselves into one þÿ ignorance ! For as from this source flow the abuses of religion, so also from this source flow the abuses of all other blessings, of talents, of riches, of power; for we abuse tilings, either because we know not their real use, or because, with an equal blindness, we imagine the abuse more adapted to our happiness. But as ignorance, then is the sole spring of evil, so, as the antidote to ignorance is knowledge, it necessarily follows, that were we consummate in knowledge, we should be perfect in good. He therefore who retaids the progress of intellect, countenniuvs crime þÿ nay, to a state, is the great/ st ot criminals; whilst he who circulates the mental light, more precious than the visual, is the holiest improver, and the surest benctactor of his race ! ( From Chambers' Edinburgh Journal) Some years ago, there used to be pointed out upon the streets of Glasgow, a man whose intellects bud been unsettled upon a very strange account. When a youth, he happened to pass a lady on a crowded thoroughfare þÿ a lauy whose extreme beauty, though dimmid by the intervention of a veil, and seen but for a moment, made an indelible impression upon his mind. This lovely vision shot rapidly past him, and was in an instant lost amidst the commonplace crowd through which it moved. He was so confounded by the tumult of his feelings, that lie could not pursue, or even attempt to see it again. Yet he never afterwards forgot it. With a mind full of distracting thoughts, and a heart filled alternately with gushes of pleasure and of pain, the man slowly left the spot where he had remained for some minutes as it were, thunderstruck. He soon after, without being aware of what he wished, or of what he was doing, found hnnself again :<t the place. He came to the very spot where he had stood when the lady past, mused tor some time about it, went to a little distance, and then came up as he had come when he met the exquisite subject of his reverie þÿ unconsciously deluding himself with the idea that this might recall her to the spot. She came not ; he felt disappointed ; he tried again ; still she did not pass, lie continued to traverse the place till evening, when the street became deserted. By and bye, he was left altogether alone. He then saw that all

his lond efforts were vain, and he left the silent, lonely street at midnight, with a soul as desolate as that gloomy terrace. For weeks afterwards he was never out of the streets, lie wandered hither and thither, often visiting the place where he had first seen the object of his abstracted thoughts, as if he considered that lie had a better chance ol seeing her there than any where else, lie frequented every place of public amusement to which he could purchase admission; and he made the tour ol' all the churches. All was in vain, lie never again placed I'is eyes upon that angelic countenance. She was e"er present to his mental optics, but she never appeared again in a tangible form. Without her essenlial presence, all the world beside was to him as a blank þÿ a wilderness. Madness invariably takes possession of the mind which broods over-much or over-long upon some engrossing idea. So did it prove with this singular lover, lie grew innocent, as die people ol this country tenderly phrase

it. His insanity, however, was little more than mere abstraction. The course of his inind was stopped at a particular point. After this he made no further progress in any intellectual attainment. He acquired no new ideas. His whole soul stood still. He was like a clock stopt at a particular hour, with some things too. about him, which, I ke the motionless indices of that machine, pointed out the date of the interruption. As for instance, he ever after wore a peculiarly longbacked and high-necked coat, as well as a neck-cloth of a particular þÿspot being the fashion of the year when he saw the lady. þÿ Indeed, he was a sort of living memorial of the dress, gait, and manners of a former day. It was evident that he clung with a degree of fondness to every thing which bore relation to the great incident of his life. Nor could he endure any thing that tended to cover up or screen from his recollection that glorious yet melancholy circumstance. He had the same ft Inurs O ot veneration for that dav þÿ that circumstance þÿ and foi himself, as he then existed which caused the chivalrous þÿ lover of former times to preserve upon his lips, as long a« he could, the imaginary delight which they had drawn from the touch of his mistress's hand. When 1 last saw this unfortunate person, he was getting old, and seemed still more deranged than formerly. Every female whom he met on the street, especially if at all good looking, he gazed at, with an inquiring, anxious expression : and w hen si ic had passed he

usually stood still a few moments, and mused with his eyes cast upon the ground, arixieusly upon women whose age and figures most nearly resembled those oi his unknown mistress at the time he had seen her and that he did not appear to make allowance for the years which had passed since his eyes met that vision. This was part of his madness. Strange power of love ! Incomprehensible mechanism of the human heart !

Thus the intellect in darkness is sickly and unlovely, being deprived of the Learns of that invigorating sun which only can restore life and beauty to its powers. Who can tell how the vegetable grows in darkness without the beams of physical light ? Its growth there is but sickly, tardy and unnatural ; it has neither internal strength to support itself, nor external beauty to recommend it to the eye. Such if the sou' which slumbers in intellectual and moral darkness. It has only the life of a vegetable: for it is turned far away ficm that spiritual light and life which can only impart vigor and durability to its faculties.

A very singular musical instrument, has been lately invented by a mechanic at Vienna. This instrument, which is called a phonomiine, is considered by musical composers and others, to he the most remarkable that ever has been produced. It is in appearance something like an organ; but the inventor has found a method, by means of numerous pipes and machinery, to cause it to emit the sound of a fine chorus of male voices. The sound of the human voice is stated to be admirably imitated by the instrument, and a person who was not aware of the nature of the instrument could not distinguish the difference. Three of these instruments were tried at the house of one of the dilattente of Vienna, and in a room adjoining was a large company of musical composers and others, and they had no suspicion but that what they heard was actually a chorus of male voices, and the beauty and precision of the supposed voices was universally admired. þÿ Voleur.
