In a beautiful and sequestered spot, in the fertile and romantic valley Lougliswecdens of county Tyrone, is still to bo seen the ruin of a cottage, now dreary and desolate in aspect þÿ the wild brier and thistle, in rank luxuriance supplying the place ol the blushing rose anil spreading jessamine which once flourished there, trained by the careful and tender hand of the voung, beautiful, and (till the fell des trover came) innocent daughter of the once happy couple, who called this spot their home þÿ a home erected for, and decorated in all the perfection of rustic beauty, and given as a marriage portion to Mary, the mother of our heroine, when she became the happy wife ol Murtha O'tShaughnessy ; and few spots had witnessed more pleasing scenes of connubial happiness than this dwelling, called after its youthful mistress "Maryvillc." es, truly, no two beings blessed willi the possession of the object of each others mutual attachment, Voung, light-hearted, and industrious, ever bid fairer for happiness than did the said Mary and Murtha, when overcoming the thousand obstacles which the parents of Mary (thinking she might look higher) had thrown in the way of their union ; they saw themselves the overjoyed owners of the lovely and picturesque Maryville. Oh ! how my heart swells at the recollection of the perfect and unalloyed happiness I've there been witness of, and recoils at the horrid thought which the retrospective view forces me, of the villainy, the baseness, the depravity of the man, who could pour the
gall of bitterness into this sweet stream of bliss. But to my tale þÿ I must not anticipate þÿ

they were supremely so, till the first, second, and part of the third year of their nuptials passed awa\ without bringing any prospect of issue. The third year, however, had not fully spent its course, when Murtha felt as il the only shade which clouded the sunshine of his happiness was dispelled bv his being greeted with a I'ttlo daughter, promising to be as lovely as her mother, bis own dear Mary, when first she captivated his youthful heart. Nothing could excel the fostering care and att ntiun which the fond parents bestowed on this first and only pledge of their mutual love.

3>AAT3X T33V1IND23X The child was animated and interesting, and as revolving years ripened her ideas, she learned to appreciate and endeavour to repay their kindness by her strict adherence to the rules of religion and propriety, of which they had shewn her so bright an example. Thus situated did the contented O'Shaughncssy's pass many a joyous year, without remorse or trouble, their only care being to train the object of their affection in the true path of virtue, and dedicate all her actions to the Omnipotent Creator, who had been pleased to grant them the consummation of their desires. Years glided by in the most perfect strain of comfort and harmony, and we find our heroine (whose name was Louisa) arrived at her eighteenth year, possessed of all the bewitching qualities which adorn her sex, and as innocent as the playful lamb that skips on the verdant sod, unconscious of its approaching doom. Adjacent to the village in which Louisa resided, lived a family of the name of Campbell, consisting of three daughters and one son. It pleased Providence to deprive them of a fond mother at an early period ; and the weakly father, worn out by length of years and a delicate constitution, was little adequate to instruct the females, or curb the unbridled passions of an unruly son. The intimacy of this family and that of the O'IShaughnessy's was the first and ultimate cause of the destruction of our heroine, and the premature dissolution of her wretched parents. The sightly appear-

desty of demeanour, attracted the attention of the youthful and innocent Louisa. They oft times would converse familiarly in the woodbine summer-house (the memorial of her own handy work, during her hours of pastime.) Their intimacy became closer, and at length the miscreant Campbell made the most ardent professions of love and affection tow ards her, which were received by the unthinking and guileless Louisa, as if thev were the true effusions of his heart. Thus blinded by the insinuating schemes of her deceiver, did she conceal from the parents the attachment she felt for him (which, she imagined, was reciprocal ;) but the sequel will shew the weakness and folly of her reliance on his honor, and her subsequent destruction. After the expiration of some months, Campbell again renewed his protestations in her regard, and privately offered his hand in marriage, which she consented to, on the condition that her guardians should approve the of match. Infamy never needs a prompter ; he agreed to abide by the decision of her parents ; but proposed in the interim that they should make some preliminary arrangements prior to their approaching nuptials, lie declared it necessary, that the wedding ring," bridal " 1 said Mary and her husband were happy þÿ dross, <Sic.. should be prow iuusly procured, and in order to effect that object, she should accompany him to t he town adjoining, to make the requisite purchases, lie studiously watched his opportunity ; 'twas a market day ; the

parents of Louisa had departed lor the village, and left their only child sole guardian of their little domicile. Campbell, urged and strengthened by the impulse of the demon, repaired to the spot þÿ persuaded the silly victim of hi« infamy to join him in a walk towards the village, vvilh the deceitful assurance of making the promised purchases; but here, gentle reader 1 must pause. Suffice it to say, the demon predominated þÿ the inhuman

ATI3 Campbell effected his hellish project, and the once innocent Louisa became the victim of barbarity and seduction. Header, picture to your mind the situation of our unfortunate heroine ; she who had been from her earliest infancy trained up in 'he paths of religion and morality þÿ the idol of fond and anxious parents, now the victim o an artful and base-hearted deceiver. The torture of her agitated feelings can be better imagined than expressed. To add to her grievances, the wietch had bound her by a cumpulsory oath to privacy, on the plea that he would marry her as soon as some domestic matters could be arranged in his family. Behoid her 1 languid and weary, returning to her fond parents, to be greeted by their wonted smiles, which she felt herself now unworthy of. She restrains her indignation against the faithless Campbell, assumes an apparent composure of ideas, rather than create the slightest suspicion in the minds of her guardians, and vainly clings to the hope that her deceiver would yet perform his sacred promise and thus save from irretrievable ruin and infamy the fame of herself and family. For many a tedious week did she anxiously expect the arrival of Campbell ; but he came not. From this period a de ep melancholy took possession of her mind; the blush which formerly tinged her lovely cheek, now began to change itself to a deadly paleness ; her piercing black eye lost its vigour and beauty, and the once captivating Louisa became as the rose whose beaut is

flown, and its leaves scattered by the rude ance of young Campbell, and his assumed mo- I north wind. The parents felt their child's decav with the deepest sorrow, and everything was administered that they imagined could give relief; Hut vain the attempt of mortal blind, Who think to cure the ills of Mind ; When once purt love lias fixed it dart 'Tis hard to eane the sickened heait. So it was with Louisa: þÿ she loved Campbell, notwithstanding his inconstancy, and still nurtured the idea of his yet fulfilling his plighted vows. Let us now return to her seducer. Did the wretch ever feel compunction for his crime ? Did the bitter pangs of remorse ever reach his callous soul ! No I he prided in the violation of injured innocence ! and never once reflected on the sufferings of his victim, or the disgrace he had entailed on the family. Some months had now elapsed þÿ Campbell, fearing that the ordinary course of nature might, erelong, in the person of his victim, make a registry of his foul deed, with the resolution of the blackest fiend, determined to rid his uneasy conscience of the load which oppressed it þÿ even by the sacrifice of his devoted fellow-creature. One dreary September evening, as Louisa was reclining in her summer-house, a prev to misfortune and soul-harrassing grief, she perceived at a distance, a figure, which on nearer inspection proved to be the long-expected, though faithless Campbell. Hope and fear alternately agitated her breast. On that ev ening her parents had gone on some business

of importance to the village, and again she was left at the mercy of the deceiver. In this dilemma, overcome bv her feelings, she sunk into a deep swoon, tin recovering from it, the wily Campbell thus addressed her : "Louisa, behold, Campbell is come to fulfil his promise; see this ling, I have procured it for the happy occasion ! The O'Sullivan's (beyond the Glen) are to be the witnesses of our nuptials ; they are in readiness; the clergyman is also prepared. Lose no time, and

tte to-morrow's sun shall gild the firmament, you will be the wife of the repentant Campbell." Louisa faintly replied, " I have been faithful to my vow ; but you" þÿ here she hesitated, and he again addressed her þÿ "Fear not, dear girl ! if 1 have been guilty I confess it; but I no;'- call heaven to witness the sincerity of my intentions !" Louisa for a time hesitated, but at length by the ardent entreaties of Campbell, she consented to (what she believed) his sincere proposal, looking upon it as the only means now lett to rescue herself and family from the disgrace which threatened them. After some little delay, they set out for their destination. The road leading to the C len was unfrequented and solitary. They journeyed on in silence, nothing interrupting the stillness of the moment, save the gushing of the mountain torrent, which took its course through the Glen, and divided itself at the level country in meandering rivulets. Campbell thus broke silence: "The night is gloomy, Louisa, but fear not ; we shall soon be at the Glen, and you arc aware that the dwelling of the CTSullivan's is immediately beyond it. After the ceremony, we will return to the O'Sullivan's, and the following morning proceed to your own cottage, where your parent- will greet you as the lawful wife of Campbell." Oh! baseness unparalleled! Monster of duplicity! Better had it been you eominitn d your vile deed openly, than lead your innocent victim like a lamb to the shambles. They had now reached the centre of the

Glen : a heavy mist came on, and they were obliged to take shelter under an imp< nding cliff. Campbell here again addressed her; " M v dearest Louisa, our present delay atibrds me an opportunity for my presenting you with a token of my attachment þÿ see this locket ; 'tis chaste gold, and contains a portion of m v hair; let me see you place it nearest your heart. The silly unsuspecting girl, threw aside the garb which protected her bosom from the rude blast, and was preparing to suspend the locket from her nock ; when, horrible to re late, the blood-thirsty Murderer buried a dagger in her snow-white bosom, at the same time exclaiming, in an unearthly tone, "Take this, fowl fool, and wed thyself to death ! t" Ere the vital spark had fled, the dying Louisa ejaculated, "mercy, 'mercy ;" but the monster heeded her not, and wrenching the weapon front the gaping wound inflicted another, as deadly. The green sod was tinged with the blood of Louisa, and she lay at the feet of her murderer, a bloody and stiffened corpse ! At this moment vivid flashes of lightning were seen to shoot to and fro þÿ the ain fell in torrents þÿ a dreadful thunder storm arose, and from the general convulsion of the elements, it would seem as if all nature shuddered at the dreadful act of the Murderer. In an unfrequented spot, adjacent to the Glen, Campbell had sunk a deep trench, and timber did he convey the mangled body of his victim. Thus was Louisa prematurely deprived of the life she received from her Creator, and

consigned to her mother earth bv the hands of a blood-stained murderer. The trench lie deposited her in was upwards twenty of feet deep: ponderous stones were heaped on it þÿ the sods replaced in their former position, and every means taken to evade the detection of the murderer. 44 But O »d, whose vengeance never sleeps, tho he delays the blow, May in one aingle moment lay the prosperous villain low." We shall now return to the parents of the unfortunate Louisa. The night o becoming o so severe, they remained at the residence of a friend till morning; but judge their anguish and horror on returning home, to find Louisa absent, lliey ran to the nearest dwelling, but

Murtha O'Shaugbnessy set out immediately for the residence of the O'Sullivans (who were old acquaintances of his family,) hoping to get some trace of his lost daughter, ll is shortest route was by the Glen. Dejected in mind, fie plodded his weary way through its intricacies, and had nearly arrived at the extremity, when in his path lav a handkerchief, which he at once recognised to have been a present from Campbell to Louisa, at an early period of their acquaintance. A thousand thoughts perplexed his mind ; he dreaded some scheme of Campbell, and hastened his way towards the dwelling of the O'Sullivans. From this period, despair and trouble reigned predominent in tlie once happy domicile of the O'Sliaughnesscy's ; the rose and jasmine, no longer trained by the hands of Louisa, became neglected and withered. The loss of their beloved child preyed so deeply on the spirits of the parents that in a few short years they were numbered with the dead. The murderer still prowled amongst men. Quicksilver v. Steam Power. þÿ The Ear! of DundonaJd (better known as Lord Cochrane) was examined last session, before the Common's Committee, on steam navigation to India. His lordship, among other matters, said he had projected þÿ a substitute for þÿsteam, as well as þÿ a new mode of propelling þÿvessels. the substitute for steam is quicksilver; and he employs it þÿ to produce power by exhausting one vessel and compressing air in another, thus forming an atmospheric plenum, and a vacuum, which will produce the same cflect as the plenum and vacuum formed by the generation of steam and its condensation þÿ This plan (superseding the necessity of carrying coals), he added, is peculiarly adapted to agitated water like the sea. The plan may h» wholly worked without fuel. The evidence and papers are too long for extract, but his lordship concludes this part of his evidence with stating that þÿ vessels fitted with quicksilver apparatus might be provided with sails of the usual kind; there would be no smoke nor any fire, and there need be no indication from their external appearance that they are equipped in any other manner than as sailing vessels. Buff Leather þÿ Formerly, when metallic armour was going out of use, but while it was still considered advisable to cover the body in battle with a better protection than ordinary clothing, a species of very thick hut pliant leather was made from the hide of the urns, or wild bull at that time plentiful in the forests of Poland, Hungary, arid the middle and southern provinces of Russia. The name by which this animal was commonly known was that of bufle,

u>Asr3<E TOawtsraastt maoanautiras &'rss. whence is derived the term buff leather as designating the hide of this animal prepared in a particular way. The Russia Company, which was chartered by Henry VIII., was obliged to import a certain number of þÿ buffe þÿhides, which were manufactured into leather for military use Real þÿbull leather would turn the edge of a sword and was pistol proof. þÿ The time of its principal use in this country was during the great civil war in the reign of Charles I., after which it gradually þÿdeclined and at length became obsolete. Besides the h ies of the urns, 1 believe those of the real butlalo of Italy were employed for the same purpose. The bull' leather of modern times is prepared from cow hide, and is used for little else than þÿsoldier sþÿbelts. Transactions of Society of the Arts.

CLIMATE OF HUDSON'S BAY. "All around the bay, but more particularly f.t Churchill Fort, the climate is extremely severe The country is' buried under frost and snow from the middle ot October to the middle of May þÿ the thermometer (Fahrenheit) frequently standing 50 degrees below Nero in January. Even in rooms at the factory, where a fire is perpetually kept up, brandy freezes into a solid substance. The rivers and lakes, which tire generally ten or twelve Let deep, are frozen to the both in. '1 be cobl, which is almost intolerable during the prevalence of north winds, is most piercing at sun rising. Europeans are obliged to observe the greatest precaution against the effects of the cold, for the air is frequently filled with small angular particles of ice, which, being driven by the wind against the face or hands, raise the skin in little white blisters, which break out into hot watery issues. The windows of the factories are made very small, and the shutters are kept closed eighteen hours out of the four and-twenty in winter. þÿ As soon as a room is thoroughly heated, and the embers of the fire burnt down, the top ot the chimney is closed so as to exclude the air, yet the walls of the apartment are generally covered with ice two or three inches thick alter the (ires go out, and this cannot be removed but by cutting it away. Notwithstanding that the resident Europeans wear a large quantity of woollens and furs, such is the intensity of the cold that they arc frequently frost-bitten ; and many of the natives tall vic-

tims to the severity of the climate. The sun is often obsenred lor weeks by thick fogs, which are caused by the watery vapours ascending from the sea. which being condensed by cold, hang all around the coast, and extend inland a considerable distance. The mock suns and moons, called Parahelia and Parasalene, appear very frequently in the coldest months. During the summer, when the thermometer is at 90. and the heat oppressive, the ground is only thawed three or four feet below the surface, so that the frost is never out of the ground Even under the 57th paralled of latitude the winter is extremely severe ; the ice on the rivers is eight teet thick þÿ brandy freezes ; and in consequence ot the cold, rocks split with a tremendous noise, equal to that of the heaviest artillery, and with a force sufficient to drive the shattered fragments to an astonishing distance. The temperature of the air is subject to the most capricious variations ; rain sometimes falls abundantly at the moment when the traveller is contemplating the cloudless serenity of the sky, þÿ while on the other hand the sun will suddenly burst forth in the midst of the heaviest showers ; and, at its rising and setting this luminary is preceded or followed by a cone of yellowish light. The Aurora Borealis is sometimes mild and serene þÿ sometimes dazzling and agitated þÿ equal in luminousncss to the full moon ; and in both cases strangely contrasted by its bluish reflection with the colour of lire which sparkles in the stars þÿ

The sea bordering Hudson's Bay is only open from July to September, and even then vast icebergs endanger the navigation of the seaman, who a' the very moment when be imagines himself at a distance from those immense floating rocks is suddenly hurried by a squall, or current (strong enough to render any vessel unmanageable), amidst an infinite number of extensive fields of ice, which every moment threaten to crush his bark into fragments þÿ Mr. Martin's His. Brit. Colonies, vol. Hi.

It is seldom that we quote from the Journal of Commerce, but the following is the conclusion of a very sensible article in reply to some following of the Evening Post: " The Post may cry coward as it likes. þÿ be conti acted for þÿ Before we make up our minds to a war with France, we shall have the courage to inquire whether the honor about which we are to fight, is really of the kind to be worth what it will cost. We slial! contemplate happy this country exuberant with prosperity, and its free and generous sons making all earth and ocean teem with their enterprise, in peace ; and its i i ties deserted its commerce annihilated, its merchants ruined, and its citizens slaughtered in war. We shall turn our eyes on our institutions of religion and learning, growing up on all sides, in peace, and vice and violence damineering in war. We shall look at the allpcrvading supremacy of our laws, in peace, and the danger to those laws by the increased of military forces and the eclat of military favorites in war. We shall look at the prospect, such as it may be, of obtaining five millions of dollars by peace, and the certainty of its loss, with five millions more by war. And finally, whoever may cry coward, we shall look at France, our old and faithful friend, contributing in no small degree to our happiness and honor in peace, þÿ but with a warlike j»opulation triple our own, a well disciplined army of three hundred thousand men, and a powerful navy,
ready to be let loose upon our coast in war, defended as wc are with half armed fortifications, and an army nominally consisting of six thousand men. If is idiotisin not to reflect on

vas»asr©23iK ma®aamair®3 ATTS. ail these things before we take irretrievable steps in pursuit of that phantom, þÿ honor" There can be no doubt, that if the rash course of the executive shall drive this country into a war with France, the journals in the service of government will be loud in iheir cry o (national honor" þÿ 'insult to our Jlug" þÿ Military " cowardly peace party traitors, " þÿ ' Ore. & tc. drc ; but they will fail in their objects. If war is unavoiLuble, the whole nation will carry it on ; there will he no division among the people ; no two parties in a contest lor the safety ot the country ; we shall all act, to a man, becoming Americans ; painiul as such a conflict is, there must be, there will be 110 shrinking horn it ; the war will be unanimously carried on, and the censure on this administration will be as unanimous þÿ the aiders and abetters in driving us into the conflict will be put dow n by the decided voice of puolic opinion, but the country will be sustained. We say this now, because the honest and patriotic elicits made by the true friends of the country to maintain peace, aie construed by the collar presses as "truckling 10 a foreign power"-" surrendering the rights of the country." While jieace, therefore, exists, let us cheerish its blessings by continually calling the attention of the people to the evils ol war. There is a large class of people who have nothing lose, to and who are louu lor war ; yet these very inen on whom this administration mainly relies for support, have 111 reality much, have every thing

to lose by war, viz. the means o! earning bread for tlieir families. W hen the President seized upon the public deposites, and a loss ol public confidence and a scarcity ol money ensued, wiro siffiered ? The poor mechanic þÿ the poor » - « - þÿ laborer þÿ the poor workman in his shop. Let our merchant vessels be once stripped and carried up to the ship yards þÿ the warehouses locked up the mechanic and cartinen þÿ unemployed þÿ the coast blockaded þÿ our merchants, traders and others retiring to the economy of a country life until peace ensues þÿ let the wharves be desolate þÿ let no buildings let the house carpenter, and the mason, and tl;< laborer be unemployed þÿ let our manufactures suspend business, and the hands oe turned loose on the world without wages þÿ and to this let direct taxation come on the people instead ol revenue derived from commerce, when we have the least means of paying the tax, and we shall all feel and all deplore the evils of war, and all lament in "sack cloth and ashes" the rash, the unjustifiable. the uncalled for threats and menances of the President, which drove us into the contest. His Majesty's steamer Spitfire, arrived from Jamaica and Antigua on Monday last. By this vessel we are informed of the loss of his Majesty's schooner of war Firefly , Lieutenant McDonald commanding þÿ having been thrown by the rollers, w hen at anchor off Belize, upon a rock, which made hole in her a bottom, when she almost immediately sunk. The commander, one midshipman, and 18 of the crew we are sorry to relate perished. His Majesty's ship Lame, Commander Smith, was to leave Bermuda 011 the 28th ultimo, for Halifax, purposely to convey the Bishop of Nova Scotia to Bermuda, and was afterwards to proceed to this island. The Admiral, it was expected, would leave early next month for England, and his place on the station be supplied by Sir Robert Waller Otway. Captain Free-mantle is to bo flag Lieutenant to the new Captain. We have been informed that the Cruiser made this island 011 the morning of the 5th instant, when she descried a suspicious looking vessel, supposed to be a slaver, and chased her to leeward of Martinique, but owing to an extremely dark night, the Cruiser lost sight of her, and was compelled to give up the pursuit.

THE PROPHET BlKD. The former religious Otaheite instilled many superstitious ideas of which the most sensible of the natives even now find it dnlicult wholly to divest their minds. A remarkable instance of this is their belief that a small bird called Oomamoo is gifted with the [lowers of speech and prophecy; and 1 hcuid Taate and Hitotte, both principal chiefs, and reckoned intelligent men, declare that th y heard this same bird prophecy an invasion of the people of Bora-Bora, adding that the chief was greatly incensed. These birds are also said to have called to persons when in the mountains, warning them of danger, and directing them which way to take. They admit, with some regret, however, that since the introduction of the christian religion, this little prophet has become dumb. þÿ Manuscript Journal of a Voyage

Apsley House. þÿ The following curious particulars relating to Apsley House; the lesidence of the Duke ot Wellington, at Hvdepark corner, are not we believe, generally known; they may, however, be relied on as tacts. As George II. was riding on horseback one day in Hyde-park, lie met an old sohG r, whom he recognised as having fought under him at Dettington, and witii great condescension fell into discourse with him. In the course of conversation the King asked what he could do for him? "Why, please your Majesty," returned the soldier, " my wife keeps an apple stall on the bit of w aste ground as you enter the Park, it your Majestv would be pleased to make us a grant of it, we might bLiJ.i a little shed and improve our trade." The King complied with his request, and the grant was accordingly given hint. The slied was erected, the situation was excellent, and the business ot the old woman eecameoi isi\ an,. , porous. After some years the old soldier died, and the grant of the late King was forgotten. Then the Lord Chancellor, attracted b\ the eligibility of the situation, removed the old woman s shed, and laid out tie ground as the site of the mansion. Alarmed, but not venturing to contend with such a high authority, she consulted with her son, who was articled to an attorney, how she should act in such an extremity. The son calmed her fears by promising to find lier a remedv as soon as the structure should he completed. When this was done he waited on his Lordship to request

some remuneration for what he ailedged to be a trespass on Lis mother's rights. The Chancellor. when lie perceived the claim to be reasonably founded, rendered a few hundreds of pounds as a compensation, which, however, under the advice of her son, the old woman rejected, and on the next interview the son demanded .£ t()0a year as a ground rent, vv hen his Lordship acceded to the proposal, and Apsley House yields to this day the above ground rent to the descendants of an old apple woman.

(From the Guiana Chronicle March 21.) Our readers will recollect that we announced to them, some weeks ago, the death ot the King of Persia, and the likelihood arising from that event of a competition lor the throne, in consequence of the number of claimants. þÿ " The late King," says the Times of the 11th ult : þÿ " Had been blessed with a progeny of some fifty or sixty sons, the eldest of whom, Abbas Mirza, was designated by him as his heir. þÿ He had, it seems, himself foreseen the disputes relative to the succession which might arise alter his death, and it was with the view of providing against them in the way which he considered most secure, that he very imprudently required of Russia, at the negociations which were followed by the treaty ofGhulistan, in 1H13, that she should formally acknowledge Abbas Mirza as the rightful heir to the Persian throne. The proposition was unhesitatingly assented to by liussia, who saw at once the means it would place in her hands of influencing matters in that country in the way best suited to her future views. A stipulation to the effect desired was therefore admitted into the body of the treaty, and the Court of i. nssia failed not to bring it forward subsequently, as a ground for requiring an extension of her power of interference in such a case as that which now occurs. It happened, however, that Abbas Mirza died some months ago þÿ that is, five or six months before his father, who, notwithstanding his former anxiety about fixing the order of succession, neglected to take similar steps on

the demise of him whom lie had chosen as heir. The consequence now is, that the son of Abbas Mirza conceives himself entitled to the Crown, and it is him the British Envoy residing in Persia has most probably acknowledge without hesitation as the legitimate Sovereign. þÿ One of his uncles, however as we have said before, disputes his claim, and being at Teheran at the time of his father's death, found but little difficulty in causing his authority to be obeyed. 'Pill lately the son of A bbas Mirza had been residing at Tabrecz, a frontier town, where the latter had died. It is at Teheran that he must be proclaimed, and thither he will be obliged to proceed."

Accordingly, the accounts received subsequently to the writing of this article in the 'Times, inform us, that the son ol Aishas Mirza, Mohammkd Scmaii, did, as was expected, proceed to Teheran, where his courage and activity soon gave the partizans of his uncle a decisive overthrow. The uncle was even so far humbled as to send a deputation to his nephew, imploring pardon Shortly after, the young Monarch left his camp amidst a salute of artillery, and proceeded in great state to the Imperial Palace. þÿ " Before the Monarch was a band of music, a detachment of cavalry with Congreve rockets, and another detachment, which escorted the standards. Then came the Court footmen, in splendid custodies, and some confidential servants. The infantry and artillery had set out some time before, and been drawn up in battle array near the Palace. The King was mounted a fine charger, the saddle <$tc , being ornamented with precious stones The Ambassadors of Russia and England, with their attendants, immediately followed the King. þÿ The Vizer, the Sehab-Zadebs, and an immense number of cavalry, closed the procession. þÿ Along the whole way several other Schab- Zadebs, noble Kadschars, and other distinguished persons had stationed themselves at intervals. The civil authorities waited at different stations for his Majesty, to sacrifice as the Schah passed, camels, oxen, and sheep, to present confectionary and break bottles, which were filled with liqueurs, and adorned with flowers. On arriving at the Palace, the

Schah took his seat on a throne richly adorned with jewels, and gave a solemn audience, to which the Ambassadors of Russia and England, the Princes and great men of the kingdom, were admitted, and had the honour to present their congratulations to his Majesty. A Mollah read the prayer, proclaimed Schan Mohammed as Padischah of all Persia, and invoked the blessings of Heaven upon him. Whenever the name of the Schah was pronounced, all the persons bowed profoundly. As soon as the prayer was ended, the Princes withdrew, and the audience ended." In this manner, all risk of a civil contest in Persia, seems for the present to be over, tne King being established on his throne amidst the approbation of the great mass of his subjects, and the complete submission of his opponents, and being countenanced, on his accession, by the cordial consent of the Ambassadors both of England and ot Russia.
